title: Solutions, Solubility and Concentration
seo_title: JSS 1 Intermediate Science: Solutions, Solubility and Concentration Worksheets (NERDC)
standard_code: JSS 1 Intermediate Science: Living and Non-Living Things
standard_text: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent; solubility depends on temperature and the nature of the solute and solvent; concentration can be expressed in percent by mass or volume and in grams per litre. (summary of the Intermediate Science curriculum, JSS 1, theme: Living and Non-Living Things)
meta_desc: Free JSS 1 Intermediate Science worksheets (NERDC curriculum, theme: Living and Non-Living Things): solutes, solvents and solubility, dissolving rate and saturation, solutions and solubility, concentration and dilution and preparing solutions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Concentration c = n ÷ V, with V in litres.
body_html:
How to think about it

A solution is a solute dissolved in a solvent. “Like dissolves like”: polar and ionic solutes dissolve in water; non-polar solutes dissolve in non-polar solvents. Most solids dissolve better in hot water, but gases dissolve better in cold water.

Molar concentration c = n ÷ V (mol/dm³). When you dilute a solution the moles of solute do not change, so c₁V₁ = c₂V₂. In a titration, a solution of known concentration is added until the reaction is complete; the moles that reacted give the unknown concentration.

Example

0.50 mol of NaCl in 250 mL of solution. Concentration?

V = 0.250 L

c = 0.50 ÷ 0.250

Answer: 2.0 mol/dm³

Example

Dilute 100 mL of 3.0 mol/dm³ acid to 600 mL. New concentration?

c₂ = 3.0 × 100 ÷ 600

Answer: 0.50 mol/dm³

Common mistakes

  • Using millilitres instead of litres in c = n ÷ V.
  • Thinking a gas dissolves better in warm water.
  • Mixing up a strong acid (fully ionised) and a concentrated acid (lots of acid per litre).
